passage:
"You lost the whole game because you're a baby," Binita said. "Even Mumma says you can't lose properly."
"I'm not a baby." Tenzin's voice shook.
"Baby, baby. Look, his ears have gone red."
"Stop it!"
"Why? You always—"
"STOP!" Tenzin's hands felt hot, and his heart thumped so hard he could hear it. He shoved the board, and the pieces flew across the rug.
"Mumma! He threw everything!"
Mumma came in from the kitchen. "Tenzin—"
But Tenzin was already running to the bedroom. The door banged. Inside, he sat against the bed, breathing fast, face burning, not even sure what he had just done.
"He always does this," Binita said.
"Let him breathe first," Mumma said quietly.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do to the board game?
qa.a: He shoved the board, and the pieces flew across the rug.

qa.q: What shows that Tenzin felt overwhelmed rather than choosing to throw the game?
qa.a: His hands felt hot, his heart thumped so hard he could hear it, and afterwards he was not even sure what he had just done.

qa.q: What does Mumma get right at this stage, and what could come next?
qa.a: She lets Tenzin breathe first instead of scolding; once he is calm she can hear both children and deal with the teasing too.

qa.q: How does Binita see what happened?
qa.a: Binita sees Tenzin as the troublemaker, saying "He always does this", without linking the shove to the teasing.

grounding: Shows a teased child whose body takes over, with a pounding heart and hot face, shoving the game and running off without a real choice.

passage: Last week I cried in the art room, and I still don't really know how it happened. I'm ten, and I hadn't cried at school since I was a small boy. Kashish kept laughing at my drawing of a horse. "It looks like a dog with a long neck," Kashish said, and then everybody at our table started saying it. I tried to say something clever back. But my heart was going so fast, and my face got so hot, that my brain just went blank. No words came. Tears came instead, big ones, in front of everyone. I pushed my chair back and walked out to the corridor. I didn't decide to. My legs just went. Later, Miss Rao found me by the drinking fountain and waited with me till I could breathe normally again. — Sachin

qa.q: What did Kashish say Sachin's horse looked like?
qa.a: Kashish said it looked like a dog with a long neck.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel when he said "My legs just went"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and overwhelmed, with his heart racing and his face hot, so his body walked him out before he could decide. 😔

qa.q: What did Miss Rao do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: Miss Rao stayed with Sachin until his breathing settled; next the teacher could talk calmly with both children about the teasing.

qa.q: What might Kashish have thought when Sachin walked out?
qa.a: Kashish may have been surprised, thinking it was only a joke, and not realised how much the laughing from the whole table hurt.

grounding: Shows a boy on the receiving end of teasing whose racing heart and hot face leave him unable to think, so he cries and walks out.

passage:
Tushar beta, come here. You shoved Aarush today and you don't know why? Let me tell you about a boy called Sachin. That was me, your Dada, when I was ten.
There was a bigger boy in our mohalla who called me "kaddu" in front of the whole cricket team. Again and again. That day my heart was going like a drum, my face was hot as a tawa, and my ears were ringing. I couldn't think one word. My hands just pushed him, hard, into the gutter.
Afterwards I sat on the step and shook. I hadn't decided anything. My body had decided for me.
So tell me, beta, what was your heart doing before the push?

qa.q: What did the bigger boy call Sachin in front of the cricket team?
qa.a: He called him "kaddu."

qa.q: What was young Sachin feeling just before he pushed the boy?
qa.a: He was flooded with anger and humiliation; his heart was going like a drum, his face was hot and he could not think a single word.

qa.q: In the story, what moment could have changed what young Sachin did?
qa.a: If he had noticed his drumming heart and walked away from the team for a minute before his hands moved, his body might not have made the choice for him.

qa.q: How might the bigger boy have felt landing in the gutter?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and angry, perhaps not realising how much his repeated name-calling had built up in Sachin.

grounding: A grandfather recalls being taunted as a boy until his body took over and he shoved the other child, showing flooding as a reaction rather than a choice.

passage:
The quiz had ninety seconds left on the board, the fan was rattling, and the whole class was shouting answers at once. Harsha's team needed one point.
Naveen leaned across. "Don't give it to Harsha, he'll just freeze like last time."
Something inside Harsha went white and loud. His heart thumped in his throat, his face went hot, and the question on the board turned into squiggles. He opened his mouth and nothing came out.
"See?" said Naveen.
Harsha's eyes filled. He shoved his chair back so hard it scraped, and walked straight out of the classroom, not even hearing the teacher call his name.

qa.q: How much time was left in the quiz when Naveen spoke?
qa.a: There were ninety seconds left on the board.

qa.q: What was Naveen's remark doing to Harsha's body and mind?
qa.a: It flooded him with panic and shame; his heart thumped, his face went hot and he could not read the question or speak.

qa.q: What could help Harsha at this stage, while he is flooded?
qa.a: A teacher could let him step outside to breathe and drink water, and talk later, since he cannot think clearly while his body has taken over.

qa.q: What might Naveen be experiencing as Harsha storms out?
qa.a: He may feel surprised, maybe uneasy, that his comment caused tears and a walk-out when he thought he was only winning a point.

grounding: Under pressure and taunting, a boy's heart races and his face goes hot, and he cries and storms out because his body takes over.

passage:
By the time Siddharth reached the colony gate, he couldn't remember what Omkar had even said. Something about his bowling, something about his dad not coming to the match, and then the other boys laughing.
He only remembered his heart. It had pounded so hard it hurt. His face had gone burning hot and his eyes blurred. He had thrown the ball on the ground and run, past the watchman, past the parked scooters, up three flights of stairs.
Now he was on the landing, breathing fast, fists tight. Ma opened the door, took one look at him, and didn't ask anything yet. She just sat on the step beside him.

qa.q: How many flights of stairs did Siddharth run up?
qa.a: He ran up three flights of stairs.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling as he ran, and why does it seem his body chose rather than him?
qa.a: His heart pounded so hard it hurt, his face burned, his eyes blurred and he could not even remember what was said; his panic and hurt took over his body.

qa.q: What turning point does Ma's response offer?
qa.a: By sitting beside him quietly instead of asking questions, Ma lets his body calm down first, so later he may be able to talk about what happened.

qa.q: What might Omkar be experiencing after Siddharth ran off?
qa.a: He may feel confused or guilty, or worried he went too far when the laughing turned into Siddharth throwing the ball and running.

grounding: After being taunted, a boy's heart races and he can't think, so he runs home; his mother lets him calm down before asking.

passage:
"Chinmay can't even catch a tennis ball," Uma said to the line outside the library. "That's why we lost the relay."

"I didn't drop it!"

"You did. Everyone saw. Right?"

A few kids nodded.

"Stop it, Uma."

"Or what? You'll cry again like in Class 3?"

Chinmay's heart was thumping in his ears. His face felt hot all the way to his hair. He opened his mouth and nothing sensible came out.

"See? He can't even answer."

"SHUT UP!" Chinmay flung his library book down on the floor and ran. He didn't stop until he was behind the water tank, breathing fast, fists shaking.

Mr Sequeira found him there. "Chinmay? Take a minute. Breathe with me." After a while Chinmay's hands stopped shaking.

qa.q: Where did Chinmay run to?
qa.a: He ran to behind the water tank.

qa.q: How can you tell Chinmay felt overwhelmed rather than choosing what to do?
qa.a: His heart thumped, his face burned, no sensible words came, and he flung the book and ran, which shows his body taking over.

qa.q: How did Mr Sequeira help, and what could come next?
qa.a: He helped Chinmay breathe and calm down first; later he could talk with both children about what was said.

qa.q: How might Uma see the moment when Chinmay ran off?
qa.a: Uma may have been surprised by how strongly he reacted, and perhaps felt a flicker of guilt or felt she had 'won'.

grounding: A child on the receiving end of teasing floods with a racing heart and hot face, throws a book and runs, with his body taking over.
